title: Adaptive UTF-8 Quick-Segmentation & Cache-Hinting to Cut Prefill CPU
creator: Aisha Raman
description:
Problem: Prefill-side CPU for tokenization and prompt preprocessing is a dominant cost for short, high-QPS requests (chat prompt prefixes and system messages). Current pipeline always runs full Unicode normalization + full tokenizer path which allocates many per-request buffers and does byte-by-byte checks. This increases median prefill wall-time and reduces throughput on hosts where CPU is the bottleneck (shared Dedicated pools and smaller private nodes).

Proposal: Implement an adaptive, two-path prefill preprocessing pipeline that routes requests through a low-overhead fast-segmentation path for ASCII/Latin-heavy prefixes and a full path for complex Unicode inputs. Key components: 1) Quick UTF-8 segmentation: fast SIMD-enabled check to decide if input is "ASCII-dominant" (~>95% ASCII or only safe BMP chars) and short (<2048 bytes), then perform byte-level segmentation without full normalization. 2) Probabilistic cache-hinting: emit a small, stable 64-bit hint (content fingerprint with tunable collision tolerance) used to consult a session-local prefix cache (LRU+TinyLFU hybrid). Hints are cheap to compute and avoid re-hashing whole strings on cache lookups. 3) Zero-alloc microbatch coalescing for concurrent prefill requests from same session: coalesce prefill tokenization work for requests that share leading bytes to reuse tokenizer state and share KV cache warmups. 4) Kernel hint propagation: expose a lightweight metadata flag from prefill path to serving runtime so kernel selection can favor short-seq, low-latency kernels when fast-paths are used. 5) Safety/fallback: worst-case correctness preserved by deterministic fallback to full unicode-normalizer + tokenizer for inputs that fail checks or on cache misses with ambiguity.

Goals/Metrics: Reduce median prefill CPU cycles by 25% on ASCII-heavy workloads, reduce p50 prefill latency by 20% at 95th percentile QPS in benchmark rig, and increase effective throughput (requests/sec) by 10% for mixed workloads. Measure tokenization allocations and GC pressure change.

Design doc & artifacts: Confluence draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Adaptive+UTF8+Quick+Segmentation+and+Cache+Hinting (design-42111)
Benchmark plan: microbench (local 8-core) then dedicated perf rig (n1-standard-style instances) comparing: current baseline, fast-path on, fast-path+cache, fast-path+coalescing.

Acceptance criteria: 1) Pass unit/integration tests (compatibility with non-ASCII languages), 2) End-to-end latency regression < 1% on random long-unicode workloads, 3) Telemetry shows >=20% CPU reduction on sampled ASCII-heavy tenants, 4) No correctness regressions in tokenizer conformance test-suite.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Spike (2d): SIMD ASCII detector + microbenchmark.
- Prototype (4d): Integrate detector in prefill pipeline, implement hint generator and in-memory session-local cache.
- Perf iteration (3d): tune hint window, cache TTL, collision policy, and microbatch coalescing threshold.
- Rollout (gradual): Canary on internal tenants -> opt-in beta -> default-on for hosted low-risk clusters.

Risks & mitigations: 1) False positives in fast-path could change tokenization for edge Unicode; mitigate by always verifying token boundaries for non-ASCII code points and by adding full-tokenizer shadow run for first N requests per session. 2) Cache fingerprint collisions: tune fingerprint size and maintain collision detection that falls back to full-key compare when mismatch suspected. 3) Increased telemetry cardinality: aggregate hints into buckets for observability and cap cardinality.

Notes: Keep implementation language-idiomatic (Go runtime path used in prefill service). SIMD code will be in a small C/assembly helper shared via CGO with clear fallbacks for platforms that don't support the optimized path.
